title: Groundwater Storage Trends in the Great Salt Lake Basin, 2002–2024
content:
ABSTRACT

Groundwater storage change in the Great Salt Lake Basin (GSLB) is difficult to quantify because monitoring data are uneven. We estimate groundwater storage anomalies over 2002–2024 with five methods: Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) total water storage minus Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) land-surface components (GRACE-raw); the same with lake and reservoir storage removed (GRACE-sw); a further correction for GRACE signal leakage, calibrated against in situ data (GRACE-Lf); the GRACE-assimilated GLDAS v2.2 product (GLDAS-2.2); and an in situ reconstruction from groundwater-level observations (GWDM). Four of the five methods show drawdowns in 2011–2016 and 2019–2022. Surface water, dominated by the Great Salt Lake, accounts for about 31% of the basin's storage signal. A leakage factor of 2.3 indicates that uncorrected GRACE captures less than half of the signal where pumping is concentrated along the Wasatch Front. Over 2011–2016, leakage-corrected GRACE indicates a groundwater loss of 13.3 ± 7.8 km3 and the in situ reconstruction 10.1 ± 1.8 km3, both consistent with an independent GPS-based estimate of 10.9 ± 2.8 km3. With a calibrated leakage factor, GRACE and GLDAS data can update the basin's storage estimate as new data are released.
